source: Light bounces off a mirror at the same angle it hits it. Light bends when it passes from air into water or glass, so a straw in a glass looks broken.
Thinking we see things because light comes out of our eyes. We see because light from a lamp or the Sun bounces off things and into our eyes.
How do you see this page? Light from a lamp or a window hits the page, bounces off, and goes into your eyes.

We see things when light bounces off them into our eyes. A smooth mirror reflects light neatly: it leaves at the same angle it came in. Light also bends (refracts) when it passes from air into water or glass.
A ray hits a mirror and bounces off at the same angle.
A straw in a glass of water looks broken where it enters the water, because light from the straw bends at the water's surface.
Light slows down a little in water and glass. Like a cart rolling from pavement into sand at a slant, it turns as it slows. Lenses in glasses and magnifying glasses use this bending.
A periscope has two mirrors. How does it let a submarine crew see above the water?
The two mirrors pass the light down and into the eye.
Light from above hits the top mirror and bounces down the tube.
The bottom mirror bounces it sideways into the viewer's eye.
Thinking light comes out of our eyes. In a dark room with no light at all, you see nothing: there is no light to bounce off things.
